title: Testing and polishing is the hardest part
author: lastplankgames
selftext:
So I'll cut through the usual "omg why does everyone hate my AI game" posts. 

  
I would say I'm about 3-4 months away from releasing my game - no trailers, no marketing, nothing. I've done the art, music, sound effects, written the story into codex entries the player will find along their journey. All of that was "easy" into comparison to testing and polishing. It's the little things like inconsistent UI, sound effects feeling off, game balance, etc.

  
My only other human playtester is my girlfriend, and she managed to beat the first two bosses on her first try - this gave me more insight into game development than what I thought I possessed. She saw things that I was completely blind too. She pointed out my bare-bones tutorial - which I thought was fine, but because I was oblivious to the fact that I knew the game so well it didn't occur to me that someone with fresh eyes wouldn't know all the mechanics from the get-go. 

  
When it comes to polishing, this is my kryptonite. I spend hours refining and checking button placements, UI consistency, animations, etc. It can be satisfying to correct these, but it's also a rabbit hole. I would suggest targeting specific areas first, before asking your AI to do a while once-over - things are bound to be missed. 

  
If I can give anyone any advice:

* Play the damn game - up until late end game
* Playtesters are probably the most important tool you have
* Polish in sections when the gameplay and mechanics are sound
* Disclose AI - you will be found out eventually and, to be honest, most gamers won't care.

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body:
AI development has actually made me pivot to polishing as I work. It has vastly reduced the amount of issues I feel i would have run into if I waited until a later milestone to begin.

But its also a great way to eat up usage. Regardless I would rather have to deal with hitting limits than smashing my head on a keyboard for a week straight because I let an issue grow in scope without realizing

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
Honestly that was always the hardest part anyways. Its easy to feel motivated when in the weeds making sprites or coding a new feature, but when you have to zoom out and really look critically at the intagibles like "the sauce" and "gamefeel" and "immersion" and "meaningful progression" you realize why a creative director with a strong vision is so necessary. Its hard to feel motivated to spool up that level for the 56th time to check if that gap jump feels good this time.

There is a youtuber dev called Blargis who made Bloodthief and has an ongoing devlog for his new game. I have learned a ton from him in terms of this esoteric aspect of development. He has several episodes dedicated exclusively to those moments of "hey im almost done! Oh shit, the game is actually not fun at all... Oh no...."

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: We build the onboarding and first 10 minutes of gameplay first with the goal of having a build we can give to strangers within the first month or so of development. I’ll keep the latest version installed on my steam deck so I can hand it to someone whenever there are a few minutes. Testing thus way has resulted in one major redesign of the core mechanics as well lots of smaller refinements and polish. It has also help us calibrate our general sense of what game we are building which helps guide the rest of development.
